1. AMD or Intel Processor?
In my opinion, you have a couple of viable CPU options with a $1,000 PC build. You could go with a newer 12th Generation Intel CPU—like, the Intel Core i5-12400—or, a Ryzen 5 5600, or the option we’ve chosen, the slightly older Intel Core i5-11400F.
The main reason we opted for the i5-11400F over the i5-12400 and the Ryzen 5 5600 is solely due to the price it comes in at. Right now, you can pick up an 11400F for ~$165 and a compatible H510 chipset motherboard for ~$85.
Alternatively, the i5-12400 and the Ryzen 5 5600 both cost ~$200 and the motherboard options are more expensive. So, to opt for one of those processors would mean to lower the budget for other components in this system. Since the i5-11400F should provide similar in-game performance to the 12400 and the 5600, we felt it was important to ensure that extra money went towards the graphics card in order to get the most gaming performance out of this build.
Of course, if you don’t mind sacrificing some in-game performance now, you could always opt for either the 12400 or the 5600 to get a boost in CPU performance.
2. RX 6600 XT: Perfect for this Budget Right Now
I think with this build an RX 6600 XT makes the most sense at the moment. I think you could fit in an RTX 3060 Ti, but you’d likely have to switch the 1TB SSD for a smaller SSD (or a traditional HDD), go with a lower-tier case, and probably downgrade the CPU as well (maybe an even older 10th Generation Intel CPU).
For me, the performance difference between the RX 6600 XT and the RTX 3060 Ti isn’t big enough to justify making all of those sacrifices—especially when you consider the real world difference between the two on a 1080P monitor.
The cheapest RTX 3060 Ti right now comes in at just under ~$650, though, so, you will need to clear a lot of room in the budget to upgrade your GPU. But, if you can afford to stretch your budget that much, it would be worth your while—especially if you plan on playing games on a higher resolution monitor, or you’re going to take full advantage of NVIDIA’s raytracing technology.
3. Is 16GB Enough for Gaming?
While the growing consensus among gamers is that “you need at least 16GB of RAM in 2022,” the truth is that it really depends on what games you are playing and whether or not you are running other games while you play your games.
Some of today’s most-played titles are games that still don’t use over 8GB of RAM (League of Legends, Rocket League, CS:GO, etc.) However, for the AAA titles that are being released, games like Elden Ring and the Tomb Raider series (as examples) are starting to utilize well over 8GB of RAM.
Fortunately, getting 16GB of RAM into a $1,000 PC build will be fairly easy. You could opt for more RAM in this build, but you’d likely have to downgrade your graphics card in order to accommodate the extra memory—and, that wouldn’t be worth it.
You could opt for a single 16GB RAM module over a 2x8GB kit, though. Then, if you want to bump up to 32GB of RAM in the future, all you’d have to do is purchase another 16GB module and pop it into your build. You’d have to sacrifice the small performance gain that dual channel memory will offer in the short-term, but if your goal is to get to 32GB of RAM, you will save money in the long term.
